prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Write mostly medium-length, complete sentences.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you type an HTTPS address into a browser and press enter, the browser first has to work out what you actually asked for. It parses the address into a scheme, a hostname, an optional port and a path, and because the scheme is https it knows to use port 443 and to encrypt the connection. Before touching the network, it checks a few local sources: its own list of sites that must only be reached over HTTPS (the HSTS list), any cached copy of the page that is still fresh, and any service worker registered for that origin that might answer the request itself. Only if none of these can satisfy the request does the browser go out onto the network.

The first network task is turning the hostname into an IP address, because routers move packets between numbers, not names. The browser looks in its own DNS cache, then asks the operating system, which checks its cache and the hosts file before querying a recursive resolver, usually run by your internet provider or a public service. If the resolver does not already know the answer, it walks the DNS hierarchy on your behalf, asking a root server which servers handle the top-level domain, then asking those which servers are authoritative for the domain, and finally asking the authoritative server for the record. The answer comes back with a time-to-live that tells every cache along the way how long it may be reused. This is why a freshly visited site often resolves instantly, while a rarely visited one can add tens or even hundreds of milliseconds. A hostname may return several addresses, and modern browsers will often try IPv6 and IPv4 in parallel and keep whichever connects first.

With an address in hand, the browser opens a TCP connection to port 443 on that server. TCP provides a reliable, ordered stream on top of unreliable packets, and it begins with a three-step handshake in which the client sends a SYN, the server replies with a SYN-ACK, and the client confirms with an ACK. That exchange costs one full round trip, which is the time for a packet to travel to the server and back, and it is the reason physical distance to a server matters so much for latency. Some sites are instead reached over HTTP/3, which runs on QUIC over UDP and folds the transport and encryption handshakes together, but a browser usually learns about that from an earlier visit, so the first request typically still uses TCP.

Once the connection exists, the browser and server negotiate encryption with TLS, which is the part that makes the address https rather than http. The client begins with a ClientHello that lists the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, carries a random value, and includes a key share for the key exchange it expects to use. It also includes the Server Name Indication extension, which states the hostname it wants, so that a server hosting many sites on one IP address can choose the right certificate. It may also list the application protocols it can speak, such as HTTP/2 and HTTP/1.1, so the choice is settled during the same exchange. In TLS 1.3 the server answers with its own key share, which lets both sides derive shared secret keys without ever sending those keys over the wire, followed by its certificate and a signature proving it holds the matching private key.

The certificate is what lets the browser trust that it is really talking to the site it asked for rather than an impostor. It names the hostnames it covers, has a validity period, and is signed by a certificate authority, which may itself be vouched for by an intermediate authority chaining up to a root that ships in your operating system or browser. The browser checks that the chain is intact, that every signature is valid, that the dates are current, that the hostname matches, and, depending on the browser, that the certificate has not been revoked or is recorded in public transparency logs. If any check fails, you see the full-page security warning rather than the site. When everything passes, both sides send a Finished message, and from then on all traffic is encrypted and authenticated with the keys they have derived. With TLS 1.3 this costs one additional round trip after TCP, and a client that has connected before may resume the session and send encrypted data even sooner.

Only now does the browser send the actual HTTP request, and it does so inside the encrypted tunnel. The request begins with a method and a path, typically GET and the path from your address, followed by headers. These include the Host header naming the site, Accept headers describing the content types and compression formats it understands, a User-Agent string, and any cookies previously stored for that site, which is how a server recognises that you are logged in. If the browser holds a stale cached copy it may add conditional headers so the server can reply with a tiny 304 response instead of resending the whole page. With HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 the same information is sent in a compact binary form rather than readable text, and many requests can share a single connection, but the meaning is the same.

The request now crosses the network again, often passing through a CDN edge server or a load balancer that terminates TLS and forwards it onward. A reverse proxy may route it to an application server, which runs your code, perhaps querying a database or calling other services, and builds a response. Or the edge may answer straight from its cache, which is much faster. The server then writes back a status line and headers, such as a 200 status and a content type, followed by the beginning of the body.

The moment the first byte of that response reaches the browser is what performance tools call time to first byte. It is the sum of everything above: DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS negotiation, the request's trip to the server, the time the server spent thinking, and the first piece of data travelling back. Knowing these stages is useful because each one can be tuned, for example with caching, a CDN closer to users, connection reuse, and faster server code.
